title: Inception
one_line: A thief who steals secrets from sleeping minds is hired to plant an idea instead, and the job unfolds across dreams stacked inside dreams.

release.value: 2010-07-16 (United States and United Kingdom; premiere 2010-07-08, London)

budget_usd.note: Wikipedia and Box Office Mojo agree on $160 million; a search summary says it was split between Warner Bros. and Legendary (not fetched from a primary page).

time_structure.summary: A heist is carried out inside a dream, then inside a dream within that dream, and so on down. Each level runs slower than the one above it, so a few minutes at the top is hours below. The film cuts between all the levels at once, and each level's wake-up cue has to land at the same moment.

themes.name: Guilt
themes.scene: Cobb's dead wife appears inside the dreams he builds and sabotages the jobs. Wikipedia's analysis reads her as a projection of his guilt over her death, which is why she keeps intruding when the team needs a clean run.

themes.name: Grief
themes.scene: Cobb cannot go home because of what happened to his wife. The whole job is a way to buy back his old life and see his children again, so a loss drives every decision he makes in the film.

themes.name: Memory
themes.scene: Nolan has said the heist framing was too shallow for a film about dream and memory, so he gave Cobb an emotional wound to carry. The dreams are built from remembered places and people, which is how the past leaks into the job.

themes.name: Time
themes.scene: In the hotel level, a fight plays out in a corridor that rotates through a full turn, while a van falls in slow motion on the level above. Different clocks run at once and the film cuts between them.

themes.name: Deception
themes.scene: The ending cuts away as the spinning top seems to wobble, leaving the audience unsure whether the final scene is real. Critics note the film keeps manipulating its characters and its viewers in the same move.

inspirations.claim: Nolan says he has been fascinated by dreams since he was a child, and the idea of a mind building a whole world you do not notice is the core appeal.
inspirations.quote: I've been fascinated by dreams my whole life

inspirations.claim: Nolan first wrote it as a conventional heist, then decided that was too shallow for a story about dream and memory, and raised the emotional stakes.
inspirations.quote: I realized I needed to raise the emotional stakes.

inspirations.claim: Wikipedia lists The Matrix, Dark City, The Thirteenth Floor, Memento, Borges and Blade Runner among influences; the link to Paprika is commonly drawn but not confirmed by Nolan.
Shone's book The Nolan Variations (2020) discusses the film's origins; cited as a book only, no excerpt fetched.

at_release.summary: Most critics admired the ambition and called it an inventive, big-budget puzzle. A minority found it too literal and rule-bound, with explanations that undercut the feel of dreaming. Audiences gave it a B+ CinemaScore.

now.summary: Online discussion has been warmer than many print reviews, and Wikipedia notes it topped many critics' 2010 lists and is often named among the decade's best. The ending's ambiguity keeps it in conversation. Letterboxd rating not retrieved (page gave no figure; ratings page returned 403).

missed.point: The levels are not flashbacks. Because a dream within a dream is not earlier than the one around it, Nolan cuts between them as simultaneous strands, motivated by the plot's deadlines rather than by character memory.
The heist plan is not explained up front as in most heist films. Exposition runs almost continuously and the plan unfolds as we watch, which is why the audience learns it alongside the team.

Nolan has said the point of the last shot is that Cobb walks to his children and no longer looks at the top, not whether the top falls. Wikipedia also records that he credited Emma Thomas with the view that Cobb no longer cares.
